newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: CANBERRA WATCH-Small labour force influence in new dole rules.
newsitem.headline: CANBERRA WATCH-Small labour force influence in new dole rules.

text.p: The Economist noted in 1995 that the British government had implemented 30 redefinitions of "unemployment" since 1979.
"In an apparent violation of the law of averages, 29 of these caused 'unemployment' to fall," the British weekly said.

In that spirit, the Australian Labor Opposition is accusing the government of trying to fiddle the books with its new rules for young people receiving the dole (which will now parade under its umpteenth name, "the Common Youth Allowance").

But an analysis of the data shows very limited scope for the new system to affect the data. As a theoretical limit, the unemployment rate could fall by 0.1 percentage point when the new system begins on July 1 1998.
From that date, people aged 16 or 17 will be able to get the dole only if they are in full-time training.
There are new means tests for young people over that age, but they seem to have no implications for their labour-force participation, so we can focus on only the 16 and 17 year olds.

So how will that affect their answers when the Australian Bureau of Statistics rings them up and asked: Did you work last week, have you looked for work in the past four weeks, and were you available for work last week? The answer to that triple question has to be No, Yes and Yes for the person to be counted as unemployed.
Of the 792,000 Australians who were unemployed in May (original data), 43,000 were aged 16 or 17.
But 22,000 of them were already attending school or tertiary education full-time, so the new rule cannot affect them.
The remaining 21,000, then, are the only ones who could move off the unemployed total and into the not-in-the-labour-force total by giving up the search for work.
But a spokesman for Social Security Minister Jocelyn Newman told Canberra Watch that 10,000 of those people were homeless and therefore exempt from the new rule.
So, at most, there are about 11,000 people out there who are currently reporting as unemployed but whom the new dole rules will force into school or training.

Even once they are in school or training, it is still possible for them to tell the statistician they are looking for work. (Indeed, half of 16 and 17 year olds who satisfy the statistician now that they are unemployed are in full-time education.)
So the new rules seem to have minimal implications for the labour force data.
